summary.countingCaveat: 734 overlapping review records: 42 lesson bodies, 69 complete questions and 623 glossary entries. These are not 734 unique atomic factual claims; corrections count field or file locations.

corrections: HPACK prefix equality needs a continuation byte; the new threshold question checks 31 as [31, 0]. HPACK and QPACK tables no longer share incorrect indexing/capacity claims.
HTTP bodyless-status/HEAD exceptions, handshake latency, cookie partition/identity and never-indexed guarantees are qualified rather than universal.
QUIC Initial confidentiality, first destination-ID choice, retransmitted information/frame boundaries, non-minimal varints, migration exceptions and QPACK blocking are explained precisely.

DNS raw labels are not universally ASCII, compressed names need not literally end in a root byte at every occurrence, NSEC intervals are not an entire NXDOMAIN proof, and a missing chain is not always bogus.
Email SPF terminology now avoids the actual shortest-path-first dictionary clash; SMTP security questions follow the authentication prerequisites.
SSH AES-GCM uses its IV invocation counter rather than the base SSH sequence number for authentication; base-packet alignment and Terrapin claims now state their negotiated-mode scope.
NTP field resolution does not establish physical clock accuracy; slew/default/era/delay claims stay conditional. RTCP compact units and modular timing are explicit.
Kademlia logarithmic progress and old-contact preference are linked to the original paper's model/trace assumptions. NAT labels do not prove reachability; STUN XOR is not encryption.
RTP markers do not prove complete frames, SRTP header visibility has negotiated exceptions, and WebRTC partial reliability is an SCTP extension use rather than a base-SCTP promise.

details.before: The header compression format for HTTP/2. It replaces repeated header fields with small indexes into a static table of 61 common fields and a per-connection dynamic table, and Huffman-codes literal strings.
details.after: The HTTP/2 field-compression format, using a 61-entry static table and a separate dynamic table for each connection direction. Literal strings can be sent raw or optionally compressed with its fixed Huffman code.

details.before: The HTTP/1.1 header option saying the sender will close the connection after this message, so it will not be reused.
details.after: The HTTP/1.1 Connection option signalling that the connection will not persist after the current response. A client sends it on the request to ask the server to close after that response; it does not mean closing before the response arrives.

details.before: End of file: a read condition meaning no further bytes will arrive from that input. On a connected byte-stream socket, recv() returning an empty byte string normally indicates the peer has closed its sending direction; a zero-length UDP datagram is a different case.
details.after: End of file or stream: no further bytes will arrive in that direction. For an ordinary TCP socket, a positive-size recv returning empty bytes after buffered data is consumed indicates peer sending-direction closure, provided no local receive shutdown occurred; zero-size reads and empty UDP datagrams are separate cases.

details.before: The encoded set of header fields carried in HEADERS (and any CONTINUATION) frames, compressed with HPACK in HTTP/2 or QPACK in HTTP/3.
details.after: An encoded group of HTTP field names and values. HTTP/2 uses HPACK and carries fragments in HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE plus any CONTINUATION frames; HTTP/3 uses QPACK and has different frame and stream rules.

details.before: QUIC encryption of the packet number and some low bits of the first header byte, using a mask computed from a sample of the encrypted payload and a separate header-protection key, so middleboxes cannot read or depend on those fields.
details.after: QUIC masking of the packet number and selected low bits of the first header byte using a separate protection key. Initial keys are publicly derivable, so this masking does not hide Initial fields from a capable observer; connection IDs and other routing information remain visible.

details.before: Checking that a peer can really receive packets at the address it claims, by sending something unpredictable there and requiring it to be echoed back.
details.after: QUIC checks that a peer can receive packets at its claimed address. Connection establishment can validate addresses through handshake or token rules; PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE checks reachability on a path during migration. Unvalidated sending is subject to amplification limits.

details.before: TCP's rule of not taking round-trip-time samples from retransmitted segments, because their ACKs are ambiguous.
details.after: TCP excludes retransmitted segments from RTT sampling when their acknowledgements cannot distinguish the original transmission from a later copy. The TCP timestamp option can remove that ambiguity, allowing the RFC 6298 exception.

details.before: An optional bit in the QUIC short header that flips once per round trip, letting on-path observers estimate RTT. It is outside header protection.
details.after: An optional QUIC short-header bit that provides an on-path RTT signal during suitable continuous bidirectional traffic. It is outside header protection; disabled signalling, application limits and packet loss can affect observed transitions.

details.before: The number in an MX record that orders mail servers: lower numbers are tried first, and servers with equal numbers are chosen between randomly.
details.after: The number ordering MX destinations: lower values are preferred. A sender randomises equal-preference destinations when it has no clear reason to favour one; connection failure can lead it to try other eligible destinations.

details.before: The fallback when a domain has no MX records at all: senders deliver to the domain's own A or AAAA address.
details.after: When a mail domain has no MX records, SMTP treats the domain itself as an implicit mail exchanger and attempts its A/AAAA addresses. Actual delivery still requires a reachable server that accepts the message.

details.before: A domain with only an A record still receives mail at that address.
details.after: A domain with an A record but no MX can receive SMTP delivery attempts at that address.

details.before: A KSK rollover publishes the new key, updates the parent DS, waits for caches, then removes the old key.
details.after: A documented KSK rollover coordinates published keys, valid signatures, parent DS changes and cache lifetimes; overlap and waiting periods depend on the chosen method.

details.before: example.com A 93.184.215.14 maps the name to an IPv4 address.
details.after: The illustrative record example.com A 192.0.2.10 maps a name to a documentation-only IPv4 address.

details.before: A mailing list adding a footer changes the body hash.
details.after: Adding covered non-whitespace body text changes the canonicalised body hash; content outside an l= prefix is not covered.

details.before: A laptop's NTP client queries a pool server every few minutes and nudges its clock to stay within milliseconds of UTC.
details.after: An NTP client polls configured time sources and disciplines its clock. Its accuracy and polling interval depend on the implementation, sources and network.

details.before: Time-based One-Time Password: a short code, usually 6 digits, computed from a shared secret and the current time, changing every 30 seconds. Both sides need roughly correct clocks.
details.after: Time-based One-Time Password: a code computed from a shared secret and a time step, commonly six digits with a 30-second step. Step length, digits, acceptance windows and replay prevention are configured protocol choices; the two sides need sufficiently aligned clocks.

details.before: A server banner SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6 tells the client it speaks SSH 2.0 and runs OpenSSH 9.6.
details.after: SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6 advertises SSH version 2.0 and the software string OpenSSH_9.6; a banner alone does not prove the installed software version.

details.before: OpenSSH 9.6 added strict KEX; a 9.5 client talking to it gets no protection.
details.after: OpenSSH 9.6 introduced strict KEX. Both peers must negotiate the extension; an older implementation may gain support through a backport.

details.before: AES in Galois/Counter Mode: an AEAD cipher mode that encrypts with AES and produces an authentication tag. Hardware AES support makes it very fast.
details.after: AES in Galois/Counter Mode: authenticated encryption combining AES encryption with an integrity tag. Some processors provide hardware acceleration; actual performance depends on hardware, implementation and workload.

details.before: A hardened server that is the only route from outside into a private network, typically for SSH.
details.after: A hardened host used as a controlled entry point into a private network, often for SSH access. Whether it is the only available route is a deployment decision.

details.before: One list in a Kademlia routing table, holding up to k contacts whose XOR distance from you lies in one power-of-two range. Nearby ranges are covered in detail, far ones sparsely.
details.after: A bounded list of contacts in a Kademlia routing table. The original distance-bucket model uses power-of-two XOR-distance ranges; Mainline DHT uses splitting identifier ranges and a capacity of eight contacts per bucket.

details.before: An ICE candidate discovered during connectivity checks, when a peer's check arrives from an address not previously signalled.
details.after: An ICE candidate learned during connectivity checks rather than initial gathering: an unrecognised authenticated request source can create a remote peer-reflexive candidate, and a successful check can reveal a new local mapped address.

details.before: An ICE candidate giving the public address and port a NAT mapped for you, learned by asking a STUN server.
details.after: An ICE candidate for the externally observed mapped address and port learned from a STUN response. That mapping need not apply to every destination or be globally reachable through all intervening NATs.

details.before: A STUN reply saying you appear as 203.0.113.5:61234 gives a srflx candidate.
details.after: A STUN response reporting 203.0.113.5:61234 supplies an illustrative server-reflexive address.

details.before: A packet with 0x2112A442 at bytes 4–7 is very likely STUN.
details.after: A STUN parser checks the magic cookie along with message type, length and other required structure; matching four bytes alone does not validate a packet.

details.before: Audio or video, such as a call, that must be played within a short deadline after capture. A packet that arrives after its playout time is useless, so such media usually runs over UDP and tolerates some loss rather than waiting for retransmission.
details.after: Audio or video with a playback schedule and limited delay budget. Data arriving after a unit’s playout deadline may be discarded for that unit, although late data can sometimes support decoder state or recovery; UDP and timely retransmission policies make different tradeoffs.

details.before: Most WebRTC browsers can send H.264 video.
details.after: With the H.264 RTP payload format, a timestamp difference of 90,000 ticks represents one second.

details.before: When delay starts rising, GCC lowers the video bitrate before packets are lost.
details.after: Delay-based congestion feedback can cause an encoder to reduce its sending target; the response depends on the algorithm version, observations and implementation.

details.before: After heavy loss, a receiver sends PLI and soon gets a fresh keyframe.
details.after: A PLI reports picture loss and can prompt recovery, but does not guarantee an immediate keyframe.

details.before: Without lip-sync, a 200 ms audio lead is obvious to viewers.
details.after: Receivers use the timing relationship from sender reports to align audio and video; acceptable mismatch depends on the application and observer.

details.before: PTP can keep clocks within a fraction of a microsecond; NTP over the internet usually manages milliseconds.
details.after: One microsecond is 1,000 nanoseconds; sub-microsecond means less than that duration.

details.before: A 2 MiB window over a 100 ms round trip caps one channel at about 168 Mbit/s.
details.after: Under an ideal prompt-credit model, a 2 MiB window and 100 ms feedback round trip give a ceiling of about 168 Mbit/s; other limits can lower throughput.

details.before: A native gRPC call uses an HTTP/2 stream containing length-prefixed protobuf messages.
details.after: A native gRPC call uses an HTTP/2 stream containing length-prefixed messages; this example uses protobuf.

details.before: Inside DATA frames, each protobuf message is prefixed with **5 bytes**:
details.after: The gRPC framing is independent of its message encoding; protobuf is the usual default, rather than a requirement of this wire protocol. Inside DATA frames, each encoded message is prefixed with **5 bytes**:

details.before: g: the tag byte value
details.after: g: the tag integer value, itself encoded as a varint; the two small tags here each fit in one byte

details.before: In words: multiply the field number by 8 and add the wire type to get the tag byte.
details.after: In words: multiply the field number by 8 and add the wire type to get the tag integer, then varint-encode it; these two tags each need one byte.

details.before: Messages have a one-byte compression flag and four-byte length before each protobuf body.
details.after: Messages have a one-byte compression flag and four-byte length before each encoded body; these examples use protobuf.

details.before: the public address and port a NAT has mapped, learned by asking a **STUN** server
details.after: the externally observed address and port a NAT has mapped, learned by asking a **STUN** server

details.before: The opposite: Kademlia keeps responsive old contacts and drops newcomers, because long-lived nodes tend to stay up and it resists attempts to fill the table with attacker nodes.
details.after: The opposite: original Kademlia retains responsive old contacts and drops newcomers. Its historical trace analysis motivated the uptime preference; the rule also impedes simple newcomer flooding without eliminating Sybil attacks.

details.before: A staged rollout inventories legitimate senders, monitors reports with `p=none`, fixes authentication and alignment, then considers enforcement. A fixed number of weeks cannot guarantee that every infrequent sender has appeared.
details.after:
A staged rollout inventories legitimate senders, monitors reports with `p=none`, fixes authentication and alignment, then considers enforcement. A fixed number of weeks cannot guarantee that every infrequent sender has appeared.

The receiver’s pass rule and the domain owner’s conformance requirements are different. For **full participation**, RFC 9989 section 8 requires domain owners to send with **both aligned email SPF and aligned DKIM**, publish the required policies, and collect and analyse aggregate reports. It explicitly forbids relying solely on email SPF when the Author Domain policy is `p=reject`. One aligned pass still suffices for a receiver’s message result; that does not make a sender’s SPF-only deployment fully conformant.

before.prompt: You're moving `corp.example` from `p=none` to `p=reject`. Aggregate reports show three sources claiming your domain: your Microsoft 365 tenant (email SPF and DKIM pass, aligned), an invoicing SaaS sending from its own IPs with `MAIL FROM:<bounce@invoicer.example>` and DKIM `d=invoicer.example`, and unknown IPs in another country (all fail). What must you do before switching?

options.text: Nothing; the invoicer passes email SPF and DKIM so it will pass DMARC
options.explanation: It passes email SPF and DKIM for **invoicer.example**, not for corp.example. Neither aligns with `From: billing@corp.example`, so DMARC fails.

options.text: Add the unknown foreign IPs to email SPF so their mail is delivered
options.explanation: Do not authorise unidentified sources merely to clear failures. Geography and authentication failure alone do not prove spoofing: investigate ownership and legitimate sending paths.

options.text: Switch strict alignment on so the invoicer's subdomain matches
options.explanation: Strict alignment makes matching harder, not easier, and invoicer.example is a different organisational domain anyway.

options.text: Give the invoicer a valid aligned DKIM signature or an aligned custom return path with email SPF authorising its servers, and investigate unidentified sources
options.explanation: At least one passing mechanism must align. Merely changing the return-path domain without email SPF authorisation is insufficient; DKIM can survive forwarding when its signature remains valid.

before.workedExample: Microsoft 365 already supplies an aligned pass. The invoicer authenticates only invoicer.example, which is unaligned with corp.example, so its messages can be rejected under enforcement. Configure and verify DKIM using d=corp.example and/or an aligned return-path domain whose email SPF authorises the sending servers. Investigate unknown sources before classifying them; their country does not establish spoofing. Monitor reports and delivery failures during rollout.

after.prompt: You're moving `corp.example` from `p=none` to `p=reject`. Aggregate reports show three sources claiming your domain: your Microsoft 365 tenant (email SPF and DKIM pass, aligned), an invoicing SaaS sending from its own IPs with `MAIL FROM:<bounce@invoicer.example>` and DKIM `d=invoicer.example`, and unknown IPs in another country (all fail). What must you do before switching? You want full Domain Owner participation under RFC 9989.

options.text: Nothing; the invoicer passes email SPF and DKIM so it will pass DMARC
options.explanation: It passes email SPF and DKIM for **invoicer.example**, not for corp.example. Neither aligns with `From: billing@corp.example`, so DMARC fails.

options.text: Add the unknown foreign IPs to email SPF so their mail is delivered
options.explanation: Do not authorise unidentified sources merely to clear failures. Geography and authentication failure alone do not prove spoofing: investigate ownership and legitimate sending paths.

options.text: Switch strict alignment on so the invoicer's subdomain matches
options.explanation: Strict alignment makes matching harder, not easier, and invoicer.example is a different organisational domain anyway.

options.text: Configure both an aligned custom return path with email SPF authorising the invoicer and a valid aligned DKIM signature; investigate unidentified sources
options.explanation: RFC 9989 section 8 requires fully participating Domain Owners to send with both aligned SPF and aligned DKIM, and forbids relying solely on SPF with p=reject. A receiver can still pass an individual message on either aligned result.

after.workedExample: Microsoft 365 already supplies aligned SPF and DKIM. The invoicer authenticates only invoicer.example, which is unaligned with corp.example, so its messages can fail DMARC. For the full participation requested here, configure and verify an aligned return-path domain whose SPF authorises the invoicer, plus DKIM with an aligned signing domain. A receiver’s individual-message pass rule remains either aligned SPF or aligned DKIM; RFC 9989 section 8 imposes stronger sending requirements, including no reliance solely on SPF with p=reject. Investigate unknown sources before classifying them: their country does not establish spoofing. Collect and analyse reports and monitor delivery failures during rollout.

details.before: The p= tag of a DMARC record asking receivers how to treat failing mail: none (monitor only), quarantine (treat as suspicious, e.g. spam folder) or reject (refuse it). Receivers may override it.
details.after: The DMARC p= tag requests none (no DMARC-specific enforcement), quarantine (suspicious treatment) or reject (rejection) for failing messages, subject to receiver discretion. RFC 9989 separately requires fully participating domain owners to send with both aligned SPF and aligned DKIM, and forbids relying solely on SPF with p=reject.
